item.title: Alejandro Godoy: "Para Xi Jinping, Egipto es un país estratégico en la Ruta de la Seda 2.0"
item.description: Por primera vez en 10 años, el presidente de China, Xi Jinping, visita Egipto. Su gira comenzó el 1 de septiembre y fue recibido por el mandatario egipcio, Abdelfatah al Sisi. La llegada de Xi conmemora los 70 años de relaciones diplomáticas entre ambos países, pero en la práctica puede significar otra cosa. Egipto es el segundo país en todo el mundo que más ayuda militar recibe por parte de Estados Unidos. Lo analizamos con Alejandro Godoy, analista geopolítico internacional y experto en China. En otro lugar y de manera simultánea, otra concentración denuncia la situación de vulnerabilidad de cientos de migrantes en Ceuta. item.title: Electric fish keep from blinding themselves with these brain cells
item.description: The brain cells you see in the above image help an African fish decode electric signals to spot prey, scan its murky surroundings and communicate with its fellows. By rigorously mapping how these cells in the electrosensory lobe are wired together, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute and their colleagues reveal how this brain area continually learns to filter out interference that would otherwise blind the fish's electric sense. They report their findings in Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mammalian genes can combine to make previously unknown mRNAs and proteins
item.description: For decades, scientists have understood that each of the roughly 20,000 genes in the human body carries instructions for a single kind of protein. Now, researchers at Harvard Medical School have discovered that instructions from different genes—even those on different chromosomes—can combine to create chimeric mRNAs that produce previously unknown, functional proteins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Astronomers from the University of Manchester and the University of the Western Cape have directly detected an extremely faint radio signal from hydrogen gas billions of light-years away, opening a powerful new way to map the large-scale structure of the universe. Using South Africa's MeerKAT radio telescope, the international team measured radio emissions from neutral hydrogen dating back to a time when the universe was several billion years younger than it is today. Fuente: Phys.org.
